Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes):  
  - Known asthma with 2–3 days of increased shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough; worsened by exertion (running/brisk walking).  
  - Minimal relief from salbutamol (blue) inhaler despite daily and prophylactic use.  
  - Preventer “brown” inhaler (Clenil/beclomethasone) used twice daily; previously 3 puffs BID; advised to increase to 4 puffs BID.  
  - Baseline (“when well”) peak flow approximately 380 L/min by recall.  
  - Hay fever.  
  - Possible eczema (patient-reported; not formally diagnosed).  
  - No prior asthma hospitalizations; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; never used oral steroids.  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):  
  - Brother: asthma.  
  - Sister: eczema.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines:  
  - Salbutamol (blue) inhaler: used PRN and prophylactically; currently daily; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  - Clenil (beclomethasone) “brown” preventer inhaler: used twice daily; previously 3 puffs BID; advised to increase to 4 puffs BID; strength not documented.  
  - Cetraben topical emollient: dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  - Hydrocortisone topical: dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  - No known drug allergies; environmental allergy: hay fever.  
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus):  Not recorded.  
- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks:  Not recorded.  
- Lifestyle: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, substance use:

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Synthesis of findings: Known asthmatic with atopic background (hay fever; family history of asthma/eczema) presents with 2–3 days of wheeze, cough, and exertional dyspnea. Frequent salbutamol use with poor relief. No sputum. Telehealth visit with no objective measures obtained; baseline peak flow when well ~380 L/min by recall.  
- Working diagnosis: Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma.  
  - Supported by transcript (wheeze, cough, dyspnea, increased reliever use, atopy) and DDx model.  
- Considerations (from DDx, consistent with transcript):  
  - Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction contributing to symptoms (onset during running; persists with brisk walking).  
  - Allergic asthma flare related to environmental/seasonal allergens (history of hay fever; no explicit trigger identified).  
  - Viral upper respiratory infection as a possible trigger (lower likelihood; no fever/systemic symptoms reported).  
  - Possible suboptimal inhaler technique/adherence contributing to poor relief (suggested by medication confusion; to be assessed in person).  
- Plan (from transcript):  
  - Increase Clenil (beclomethasone) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting in-person review.  
  - Use salbutamol (blue) inhaler as needed up to every 2–4 hours; high-frequency need indicates poor control.  
  - Book in-person GP appointment in the next few days for chest examination and peak flow measurement; treatment may include oral steroids and/or antibiotics depending on findings.  
  - Seek urgent care in the emergency department if breathing worsens before review.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma – High likelihood: Classic triad of wheeze, cough, exertional dyspnea with increased reliever use and poor relief in a known asthmatic with atopy.  
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction – Medium likelihood: Symptoms began during running and recur with brisk walking; common in asthmatics.  
- Allergic asthma flare – Medium likelihood: Atopic background (hay fever; family history) with potential environmental trigger, though no specific exposure identified.

- Missing but clinically expected elements: No vital signs, oxygen saturation, or peak flow obtained; no BMI/anthropometrics; immunization review not performed; smoking/alcohol/substance use not documented; inhaler technique not assessed; hearing, vision, mood screening not documented; preventive screening (cervical screening, mammography, fecal occult blood test, bone density) not addressed.  
- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None regarding clinical content. Note: Patient’s DOB (1996) indicates age <55; this template category (Adults 55+) does not match patient age (conflict noted).  
- Transcript quality notes: Telehealth encounter; several unclear/inaudible segments; initial medication list unclear but clarified to include Cetraben and hydrocortisone topical agents; inhalers referred to by color (“blue,” “brown”) with brand Clenil identified for preventer.
